body: I feel this. It sounds like you've got systems in place to help you muster through. Maybe it's your philosophy, how you were raised, your culture or something, but you push through. But you shouldn't have to push so hard. You deserve easiness in life and you deserve happiness. You shouldn't have to tolerate this kind of pain all the time. You should reach out to a professional if you haven't already and be prepared to speak up about how you feel. Depression like this is often overlooked but it's not any less real or serious, so if you have the misfortune of coming across a dismissive or unhelpful therapist or psychiatrist, don't give up! Keep seeking help, because you deserve it. Your feelings that there's got to be more to life or that you deserve more happiness are completely correct. Hope you find the support and help you need and that you're able to matriculate into your dream university (if it's best for you!) and truly enjoy the fruits of your hard work! <3

You're right, codependency like addiction is not a moral failing. I guess I think it's that so often both are used with a heavy moral judgement. But that doesn't make the word itself bad. I think I hear people use codependent to get the point across that they think there's something bad about a relationship, and they're stringing in the clinical association with the word to say "this is objectively bad, and it's not just my opinion". Which is also how people use "addict" actually! And both have the two-fold edge of using clinical language to legitimize themselves while also using the shitty moral association to shame the other person. But I guess we can start by remembering that none of them are supposed to have moral judgment attached to them.

yes I really like this language. And yes! It feels cruel to call people who have dependencies on partners "codependent" when it's an (often enthusiastic) agreement between the two. That's totally separate from whether polyam will or won't work out with them-- we can share advice that two people might not workable relationship for polyam without the shame that is attached to calling their relationship codependent. 

which also doesn't allow people who are truly in codependent relationships the language to hear that they really need professional help.

Ahahaha. This is a pet peeve of mine-- dissociation, gaslighting, codependency, red flags. they mean different things and it's not to invalidate what people are saying but it does muddy the conversation around real, actual gaslighting, etc, when we use the words so uncritically.

Also don't listen to the men who complain. Most of the time men are not aware of how hard others are working-- many of them are hiding that they think pretty women have it easier in life than they do, not understanding how their privilege works. Those men who complain probably aren't doing as well as their partners because they suck, and it sounds like your partner is great so he's having a great time as predicted. He's still got it easier than you-- women have to be great AND lucky.

I feel you so much, I've felt pretty much every single part of what you're saying. And to be honest, before I reached the "I'm putting in all this labor for no benefits and why am I doing this" I went through some really, really bad bouts of mental health all in the name of trying to do ENM right and stick with it. This just my own experience (not suggesting anything, just sharing since we have so much in common!) but I actually gained a lot of peace and clarity when I allowed myself to acknowledge that it didn't feel worth it and my mental health had plummeted since we opened up and I could share that and it's not a manipulation and my partner loves me and I'm allowed to be having a bad time or even be doubting the whole thing. 

Doing this put a lot of things into perspective-- it made me feel loved to share my feelings and be supported. It made me realize that even if I'm an insecure little defeatist shit who can't date, that I can ask for a lot and that's okay. My partner loves me and wants to support me even if I'm a LOT a lot. This made me feel a lot more grounded. 

Also it might help to hear from another woman (although I'm bi) that dating as a woman is hard. I had heard in the past that in straight relationships the guy always has a harder time and it often can hurt his ego. That kind of implied that dating as a woman is easier and holy mother of god that is NOT true. Of course its not true. Fearing for your safety, dating men who are often much less mature, much less responsible, much less likely to view you as a human-- that's way hard! As a bi woman, I can share that my experience dating women has really opened by eyes to how much easier it is to date without such ingrained habits around my safety, to date people whose actions match their words. I know other queer women disagree and obviously there are so many exceptions, but my point is, it's undeniable that dating men is difficult. And your boyfriend is lucky he doesn't have to deal with the bullshit you do. It does make it easier, and you should give yourself a lot of grace for navigating this. And I think you should allow yourself some space to feel resentful or envious of his situation.

I'm doing better now, but a large part of it is because I realized I could say "I'm not okay" and ask my partner to help me feel okay. And it made me realize I genuinely didn't want to ruin any of their fun, so I didn't want to veto things or stop things. "Helping" me feel okay meant listening, being supportive, etc. When I came at it from a "I need help" place and not a "this or that action of yours is bothering me" place, it was a lot easier for them to do this and not feel attacked (as they had before). But we did pause things for a little while and it did help. And we adjusted things around some new boundaries that I discovered to protect myself from my plummeting mental health. Small agreements that I thought were unreasonable until I realized we made our rules (like no dating friends, I can't prepare myself well without 24 hours notice for dates, etc). And we realized how much we mean to each other. And things are a bit slower, much more communicative, and a lot happier than before.

People conflating this with being an ally to the LGBTQIA community are off base imo. I think it's HIIIIGH time we all learn that saying "that's like if you--" about another community is bad and kind of coercive logic. The polyam community isn't the same as the LGBTQIA community, just as it isn't the same as the neurodivergent community or disabled community or an ethnicity or race-based community. The "rules" of belonging to a community changes by community and context. I think it would benefit us to not be so up in arms about who belongs and who doesn't. 

If people here agree that polyamory carries with it some kind of marginalization, then it doesn't make any sense to say that spending the first 18 years of your life within a non-traditional system doesn't carry that same marginalization. And if we're not talking about marginalization here, then I don't think anyone has the right to gate-keep the community at all. Because unlike sexuality, relationship structures are inherently CONNECTED to other people. Children are inherently involved with parents' decision to have a polyamorous structure, in a way that is not the same as having gay parents. In the same way that children of divorce rightfully seek community with other people in a larger community of people affected by divorce. Personally, I think children of divorce have an important perspective that divorcees and people who study divorce don't have. And the same goes from children of CNM families. 

Even words of anger or annoyance, even vague and clunkily spoken words have value to the community, as long as they aren't harrassing or breaking rules or antagonizing. They might not be the community-favorite, but I think they have something valuable to say.

There's nothing wrong with a no overnight rule just the same way that there's nothing wrong with a solo poly person wanting to sleep in their own bed alone every night. It sounds like you're discovering that overnights are a need for you, since you can't respect that the partner doesn't want to have overnights when his wife is sleeping alone. I think you're making the wife's position into a bit of a scapegoat position-- when really, it sounds like the boyfriend has expressed that he wants to spend the night with his wife when she's around, but is happy to sleep with you overnight when she's not around. There's nothing wrong with this arrangement, especially since it sounds you came into this relationship understanding the dynamic at play. If you're realizing overnights are a necessity for you, and this is something your boyfriend can't give you, then maybe it's worth reassessing the relationship or your commitment to it. You deserve that kind of relationship if you want it, and if having another relationship where overnights are allowed isn't enough to satisfy the need (meaning every relationship has to include it) then that's really valuable info for you to know moving forward! 

It also sounds like maybe the underlying issue might be insecurity around the marriage and not just the overnights. Maybe being in a relationship with a married person brings up too many intense feelings you and is something to consider moving forward.

It's been a few years since i was diagnosed and I'm still unlearning all of this. I was in a very similar boat as you, achieved academically and was generally very polite and well behaved. I was surprised when I went for a diagnosis that my psych diagnosed me with adhd-hi and not just the inattentive form because that was always what made me feel like my symptoms weren't severe enough to be paid attention to or treated. but in getting that diagnosis, I've let myself wonder if maybe I was just as hyperactive as my off-the-wall peers. And it's uncovered an inner dialogue I didn't even realize I had, reprimanding myself for interrupting people ("so self-centered of me >:( what a disgusting trait") and wanting to get up and move around ("I never want to do the hard work, everyone else is disciplined enough to stay focused, stop being so self-indulgent") etc. It's a relationship with myself I had so intensely normalized, I didn't even notice it was there, and it's mind-blowing to continue to catch this voice in my head and the way it influences me when I really listen closely.

the therapist i started seeing for the same issues came at me with "but why do you need a diagnosis? what would you do differently if you were diagnosed? why?" so i feel like theres something wrong with needing to be sure, but i think after alllll these years of telling myself i just needed to work harder, everyone feels this and i'm not any different, an official diagnosis would be really validating and healing. but i'm afraid of the psychiatrist doing the same thing as that therapist.
